Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia Fraternity 1 Guide to Ceremonies (Excerpt) FOUNDER’S DAY CEREMONY (2019) In Honor of the Sinfonia’s Founder and First President, Ossian Everett Mills Ossian Everett Mills Ossian Everett Mills was born to Andrew and Maria Mills of Thompson, Connecticut on February 15, 1856. As early as 1879, he went to Boston where he was eventually employed in the business office of the New England Conservatory by Dr. Eben Tourjée, founder of the institution. Mills rose eventually to be bursar, the position he held at the time of his death, and the one through which he had been known to thousands of Conservatory teachers and students. “Mills impressed all with whom he came into contact with his quiet sincerity and determination, and his beliefs had a profound influence on the early course of the Fraternity. He quickly earned the respect of the conservatory students who eagerly sought his advice.”1 In 1898, Mills founded the Sinfonia Club at the conservatory, which was destined very soon to become Alpha Chapter of Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia Fraternity of America. He was elected an honorary member of the club at its first meeting on October 6, 1898. On November 14, 1898, the chapter elected him treasurer, an office which he held for many years afterward, and appointed him to the group named to initiate the club’s officers. Although the first initiation of members took place on November 28, 1898, Mills was not initiated until the following meeting on December 13. Often referred to as the “Father of the Sinfonia,” Mills had been a familiar figure at annual conventions until his last years, when his work would not permit his leaving Boston. He served the Fraternity as Supreme President from 1901- 1902 and 1904-1905 and was elected “Honorary Grand Supreme President for Life” in 1904. In 1954, former Supreme President Percy Burrell recalled his long friendship with Mills. He noted above all Mills’ humility and the fact that Mills became somewhat uncomfortable when given recognition as having “planted a seed in the hearts of some young men studying music at the New England Conservatory in Boston back in 1898, that had blossomed forth into a national brotherhood that year after year had been making its impress throughout the country…” Burrell wrote further: “I can still see what seemed to be a wistful yet joyous expression on his face whenever this thought was expressed in his presence.”2 Ossian Mills died from pneumonia at his home in Wellesley, Massachusetts on December 26, 1920. He had been ill for only a few days, and “his death came as a great shock to his associates and assistants to all of whom was familiar the story of the great service which he rendered in the earlier years of the school” and which he “unremittingly continued” during his latter years.3 He is buried in the family plot of a small, wooded cemetery in Thompson, Connecticut. At the meeting of the Alpha Chapter on January 4, 1921 a committee was appointed to draw up the following resolutions commemorating the service: RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED BY ALPHA CHAPTER On the Death of Brother Mills Whereas, We have lost by death our brother, Ossian E. Mills, Founder and honorary Supreme President of Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia, a man whose sterling character and unselfish service had made him beloved of all Sinfonians: Be it Resolved, That we the members of Alpha Chapter, Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia, express our profound sorrow at the great loss of Brother Mills from Alpha Chapter and the Fraternity at large, which will always remain a living monument to his service and vision. Be it further Resolved, That we extend our deepest sympathy to the bereaved family of Brother Mills with the hope that their sorrow will be lightened by the knowledge of the fact that his work among us still lives. Mills’ grave is marked by an unobtrusive monument erected by the Fraternity and dedicated on December 23, 1928. The monument bears an epitaph which describes the three qualities which characterized Mills’ life: “SACRIFICE, AND SECRET ZEAL, AND TRUTH.” The Installation Service presented at the dedication of this monument was revised for 1 Klint, Edward, "A Portrait of Ossian Everett Mills, the ‘Father of the Sinfonia’," The Sinfonian XXXIV, 1 (October, 1984): 10. 2 Ibid. 3 “Ossian E. Mills,” The Conservatory Bulletin II, 12 (January, 1921): 4.

Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia Fraternity 2 Guide to Ceremonies (Excerpt) the October 5, 1998 Memorial Service which was presented as part of the centennial observance of the Sinfonia’s founding. This Founder’s Day Ceremony is based on these previous services and honors the man to whom the Brotherhood of Sinfonia is a living monument. Staging and Presentation Dress for this ceremony is formal pin attire, with all brothers present wearing shirt and tie (and suit or jacket, if desired) and wearing the fraternity pin. A small table or stand is covered with a plain white cloth and is placed in the center of the room. Stage left of the table (to the right of the table as viewed by the audience) is a lectern from which the Assistants may read their respective portions of the ceremony. Stage right of the central table is a row of seven chairs in which the Assistants are seated in order when not standing at the lectern. During the ceremony, each Assistant lights a white candle from a central white candle placed by the presiding officer. These candles are placed one by one, around the central white candle, in the following triangular formation: 1 6 5 2 4 3 For presentation of this ceremony, the following statistics must be secured from the National Headquarters: Number of most recent national convention Location (city and state) of most recent national convention Date of most recent national convention Number of deceased Sinfonians Current number of active Sinfonians Current number of active chapters Current number of living alumni Total number of living active and alumni Sinfonians Total number of chapters ever chartered Total number of states in which chapters have been chartered

Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia Fraternity 3 Guide to Ceremonies (Excerpt) CEREMONY I. “Sinfonia Hymn” (Beethoven) (During this song, the presiding officer approaches the central table and places a white candle at its center. He then takes his place behind the lectern.) II. Presiding Officer We are met on this, the 121st anniversary of the Sinfonia’s founding to pay homage to the memory of its founder and first president, Ossian Everett Mills. Those who are present in the flesh are but a small portion of that large brotherhood which the vision and activity of this great spirit called into being. As the organization which he founded contemplated the inclusion of many men devoted to the uplift of mankind through the beauty and power of music, it is fitting that more than one voice should add its word of tribute. I call first, therefore, upon three of our brothers who represent the past, the present, and the future of the Sinfonia. III. Hymn to the tune “Adeste Fidelis” Here walked the master, by hope and faith attended, He brought Music down to earth from Heaven on high, As brother Exemplars, with lyres and voices blended, We dedicate our tribute (three times), beneath arching sky. IV. First Assistant I am the spirit of the past, extending from the first informal meeting of a group of the “old boys” at the New England Conservatory on September 22, 1898, to the 56th national convention held in New Orleans, Louisiana little over 1 year ago. Through me speak the voices of those who, with Brother Mills, constituted the founders of the Sinfonia: Robert Thomas Bayley, Frederick W. Briggs, George A. Burdich, Henry P. Dreyer, George Sawyer Dunham, Archibald M. Gardner, John Frederick Hartwell, William C. Holcomb, Albert J. Stephens, Frank Leslie Stone, Shirley Francis Stupp, William Elmer Tanner and Delbert Lorenzo Webster. I would recall the earnest, devoted, and brotherly discussion and activity in these men who made our present organization possible. I would record the names of the first national officers: Ossian E. Mills, supreme president; George C. Williams, supreme vice president; Ralph Howard Pendleton, supreme secretary; Gilbert Raynolds Combs, supreme treasurer, and Percy Jewett Burrell, supreme historian. All of these men excepting one served at some time as supreme president, and the single exception served as supreme secretary and supreme historian in two successive terms. Here were a group of vigorous, capable men. In their names, and in the names of over 14,600 departed Brothers who, in their lifetimes, tread upon the paths set out before us by our Founder, I place this Light by which the past would honor the memory of Ossian E. Mills. (First Assistant places white candle upon central table.)

Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia Fraternity 4 Guide to Ceremonies (Excerpt) V. Second Assistant I am the spirit of the present, extending from the Sinfonia’s 56th national convention to the beginning of its 122 nd year. To more than 6,000 collegiate members in 249 chapters, and to more than 119,000 alumni Sinfonians scattered throughout the land, the name of the founder is as a talisman of brotherly devotion. We are bound together by the bonds of brotherly love, stronger than bands of steel, ever keeping in mind the aim and purpose of the Fraternity as expressed by its founders: “The Sinfonia stands for the development of the best and truest fraternal spirit; the mutual welfare and brotherhood of musical students; the advancement of music in America; and a loyalty to the alma mater.” In the words of Father Mills, “Let all Sinfonians commit these beautiful words to memory. Yea, more, let us write them on the tablet of our hearts that they may bear fruit in our lives.” In the names of nearly 125,000 collegiate and alumni Sinfonians, I place this Light by which the present would honor the memory of Ossian E. Mills. (Second Assistant places white candle upon central table.) VI. Third Assistant I am the spirit of the future. To all of us humans the future is a closed book except that we know it is a continuation of the present, just as the present flows out of the past. We, therefore, can speak of the Sinfonia of the future only in terms of what has been. From the organizing of the first chapter in Boston to the present day, 453 chapters have been chartered in 44 states across the nation, and the District of Columbia. The scope of the Sinfonia’s mission is national, and its influence is felt from ocean to ocean and from lake to gulf. Onward is our watchword; the future is our field; and as we march forward, the new ground we gain must be held by fidelity and vigilance. In the name of this ever-increasing army of young manhood in music, I place this Light by which the Sinfonia of the future would honor the memory of Ossian E. Mills. (Third Assistant places white candle upon central table.) VII. Presiding Officer As a great tributary draws its water from earth and sky, from springs and rain, from small stream and great, from rivulet and lake, so does the course of the Sinfonia gather its forces from past, present and future. Therefore, my brothers, in the name of the (chapter name)_____ Chapter/Province ___, I accept these tributes. VIII. “Sing of Sinfonia” (Plank) IX. Presiding Officer Upon the tablets of our hearts are cut in letters which shall long endure these significant words: “Sacrifice, and secret zeal, and truth.” These represent three of the outstanding characteristics of the man whom this tribute would honor. For Sinfonians these words have particular significance, and I now call upon three brothers to interpret them.

Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia Fraternity 5 Guide to Ceremonies (Excerpt) X. Fourth Assistant The man who loves but himself can never attain to the full measure of manhood nor reach the supreme heights of his art. Each one must make a supreme personal endeavor to elevate others to the place where they may enjoy all that is true, beautiful, and abiding. Our rights, our duties, our responsibilities, our interests, and our thoughts must be mutually helpful. This was the spirit of thoughtfulness to others even at the expense of his own time, effort, and strength, which found expression in our beloved first president. In memory of this spirit of sacrifice, I place this Light to honor the memory of Ossian E. Mills. (Fourth Assistant places white candle upon central table.) XI. Fifth Assistant Those who continually uphold the beauty and power of music, who ceaselessly pour out their souls to win the world to harmony, must some time, somewhere, have recourse to kindred souls with whom in secret they can commune and renew their zeal. With them they can share those dreams which are too deep for idle words, those inspirations which are too intense for thoughtless speech, and those visions which are too exalted for the casual small talk of the streets. The desire to make this communion easier for earnest music students found expression in our beloved first president. In memory of this spirit of secret zeal, I place this Light to honor the memory of Ossian E. Mills. (Fifth Assistant places white candle upon central table.) XII. Sixth Assistant Music has been called the handmaid of religion, and its devotees are known as priests of melody and solvers of discord. Who is fit to enter upon this calling? He who is loyal in all human relations, he who keeps the straight course of integrity, he who has burned from his being the dross of infidelity and untruthfulness and has attained to the pure gold of refined character. This spirit of sincerity, of directness, of truth, found expression in our beloved first president. In memory of this spirit of truth, I place this Light to honor the memory of Ossian E. Mills. (Sixth Assistant places white candle upon central table.) XIII. Presiding Officer Every living organism is greater than the sum of its parts, and no recital of the virtues of a man can give a complete picture of him. Sacrifice and secret zeal and truth were three of the strong characteristics of our first great brother, but he was more than they represent. It is to him that we can most truly apply the phrase, “the manly musician and the musicianly man.” Today we do homage to the memory of those virtues which were his, and which, through brotherhood, shall be ours. With this as our ideal, the Sinfonia serves as a living monument to the memory of our founder and first president, Ossian Everett Mills. To this monument, may all the valiant youth continue to draw near for centuries to come, to sing as one, though thousands raise the song.
